## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes standardized methods for surveying pollinator
communities at EA Program field sites using timed visual observations
and passive pan traps. Pollinator surveys document the diversity and
relative abundance of bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, and other
flower-visiting insects, providing data for assessing habitat quality,
restoration success, and the effects of land use on pollination
services [@potts2010; @lebuhn2013].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Standardized pollinator observation surveys and pan
  trap sampling at all EA Program terrestrial field sites with
  flowering vegetation, including the Bernard Field Station, campus
  landscapes, restoration sites, and agricultural study areas
- **Does not apply to:** Targeted bee nesting surveys; hive management;
  pollen analysis (palynology); pollinator genetics or molecular
  identification (though specimens collected here may be used for
  those purposes); aquatic insect sampling (see
  [SOP-F610](SOP-F610-macroinvertebrate-sampling.qmd))
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites with floral resources


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve survey design and collection permits            |
| Trained Personnel | Conduct surveys and process pan trap samples per this SOP |
| New Students      | Complete training (insect identification and sting safety) before independent work |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Bee and wasp stings are the primary hazard. Personnel
  with known Hymenoptera allergies must carry a prescribed epinephrine
  auto-injector (EpiPen) and inform the field lead before every outing.
  Africanized honey bees may be present at some Southern California
  sites.
- **Chemical:** Soapy water in pan traps (low risk). Ethanol (70%) used
  for specimen preservation is flammable.
- **Physical:** Heat exposure during mid-day surveys. Uneven terrain.
  Pan traps may be trampled by people or wildlife.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Light-colored clothing (dark colors attract bees)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] EpiPen (if allergic; inform field lead)
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (when handling preserved specimens)

### Permits

Insect collection may require a Scientific Collecting Permit from the
California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) depending on the site
and target taxa. The PI must confirm permit status before fieldwork. No
permit is needed for observation-only surveys.

### Emergency Procedures

For anaphylactic reactions to stings: administer EpiPen, call 911,
begin CPR if needed. Refer to
[SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd). If encountering
an aggressive swarm, walk calmly and quickly away from the area; do
not swat or run erratically.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

### Timed Observations

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Stopwatch or phone timer              | For standardizing observation periods    |
| Hand lens or magnifying glass         | For in situ identification              |
| Camera (macro-capable or phone)       | For photo-documenting pollinators on flowers |
| Field notebook or data sheet          | Pre-printed observation form (Appendix A) |
| Insect field guide                    | e.g., *California Bees and Blooms* (Frankie et al.) |
| iNaturalist app (smartphone)          | For photo-based identification; see [SOP-F602](SOP-F602-inaturalist.qmd) |
| Compass and GPS                       | For recording transect or plot locations  |

### Pan Traps

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Plastic bowls (12 oz, 3.25 in rim)    | White, fluorescent blue, and fluorescent yellow; one of each color per station |
| Fluorescent spray paint (blue, yellow) | For painting white bowls; use UV-bright paints |
| Unscented liquid dish soap            | 2--3 drops per bowl (breaks surface tension) |
| Water                                 | To fill bowls approximately 2/3 full     |
| Wooden stakes or wire stands          | For elevating bowls to canopy height in tall vegetation |
| Fine mesh strainer                    | For removing insects from bowls           |
| Whirl-Pak bags or vials               | For storing collected specimens           |
| 70% ethanol                           | For preserving specimens                 |
| Forceps (soft-tipped)                 | For handling specimens                   |
| Labels (waterproof, internal)         | For vial and bag identification          |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Survey Timing and Conditions

Conduct pollinator surveys during peak pollinator activity:

- **Time of day:** 09:00--15:00 local time (peak flight activity)
- **Weather:** Sunny to partly cloudy; wind speed below Beaufort 4
  (< 5.5 m/s); temperature above 15 C. Do not survey during rain,
  heavy overcast, or high winds, as pollinator activity drops sharply.
- **Season:** During peak bloom at the study site. In Southern
  California, this is typically March through June for most habitats,
  with a secondary bloom in fall for some species.
- **Flowering requirement:** Surveys are only meaningful when flowers
  are present. Record the dominant flowering species and estimate
  floral density (flowers per m^2^) at each survey location.

### 6.2 Method A: Timed Observation Surveys

Timed observations record pollinator visits to flowers along a fixed
route or within a fixed plot during a standardized time period
[@dicks2016; @lebuhn2013].

**Transect walk method:**

1. Establish a transect (typically 50 m x 2 m, or a 100 m x 1 m
   corridor) through the area of interest. Record the transect
   coordinates per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd).
2. Walk the transect slowly at a pace of approximately 10 m per minute.
3. Record every pollinator observed visiting a flower within the 2 m
   band on either side of the transect center line (or 1 m on each
   side for a 2 m wide transect).
4. For each observation, record:
   - Pollinator group or species (see Section 6.4)
   - Flower species being visited
   - Behavior (nectaring, pollen collecting, resting)
   - Time of observation
5. Complete the transect in 10--15 minutes. Do not stop and wait for
   pollinators; maintain a steady pace.
6. Repeat the transect 2--3 times per sampling event, spaced at least
   30 minutes apart.

**Focal flower observation method:**

1. Select a flowering plant or patch and observe for a fixed period
   (typically 10 minutes).
2. Record every pollinator that visits any flower on the focal plant
   during the observation period.
3. This method is useful for comparing visitation rates among plant
   species or treatments.

### 6.3 Method B: Pan Trap Sampling

Pan traps passively capture flying insects attracted to colored bowls
[@lebuhn2013; @westphal2008].

1. At each sampling station, set out three bowls: one white, one
   fluorescent blue, one fluorescent yellow. Space bowls approximately
   3 m apart.
2. Fill each bowl approximately 2/3 full with water. Add 2--3 drops
   of unscented dish soap (this breaks the surface tension so insects
   sink).
3. Place bowls at the height of the surrounding vegetation canopy:
   - In short grass or bare ground: set directly on the ground
   - In tall vegetation (> 30 cm): elevate on stakes or wire stands
     so the bowl rim is at canopy height
4. Deploy traps in the morning (by 09:00) and retrieve after 24 hours.
   For shorter deployments (4--6 hours), retrieve in the afternoon.
5. Pour the contents of each bowl through a fine mesh strainer.
   Transfer captured insects to a labeled Whirl-Pak bag or vial with
   70% ethanol.
6. Label each vial with: site, station number, bowl color, date
   deployed, date retrieved, and collector initials.
7. Return specimens to the lab for sorting, pinning, and
   identification.

::: {.callout-note}
Pan traps are biased toward small- to medium-sized bees and may
under-represent large-bodied bees (bumble bees) and butterflies
[@westphal2008]. Combine pan traps with timed observations for a
more complete picture of the pollinator community.
:::

### 6.4 Pollinator Identification

Identify pollinators to the finest taxonomic level possible in the
field. At a minimum, assign each observation to one of the following
functional groups:

| Code | Group                    | Examples                          |
|:-----|:-------------------------|:----------------------------------|
| HB   | Honey bee                | *Apis mellifera*                  |
| BB   | Bumble bee               | *Bombus* spp.                     |
| SB   | Small native bee         | *Halictus*, *Lasioglossum*, *Ceratina* |
| LB   | Large native bee         | *Xylocopa*, *Megachile*           |
| BF   | Butterfly                | All Lepidoptera                   |
| SF   | Syrphid fly (hover fly)  | Syrphidae                         |
| OF   | Other fly                | Bombyliidae, Tachinidae, etc.     |
| BT   | Beetle                   | Flower-visiting Coleoptera        |
| WA   | Wasp                     | Vespidae, Sphecidae, etc.         |
| OT   | Other                    | Hummingbirds, moths, ants         |

Photograph all specimens that cannot be identified in the field.
Upload photos to iNaturalist per
[SOP-F602](SOP-F602-inaturalist.qmd) for community-assisted
identification.

### 6.5 Specimen Processing (Lab)

1. Sort pan trap specimens by order under a dissecting scope.
2. Pin bee specimens following standard entomological practice (pin
   through the right mesopleuron) and label with locality, date,
   collector, and determination.
3. Store pinned specimens in a labeled unit tray in the insect
   collection.
4. Specimens can be submitted to a taxonomic specialist or DNA
   barcoded (COI) for species confirmation.


## 7. Quality Control

- Record weather conditions (temperature, wind, cloud cover) at the
  start and end of every survey. Do not compare data collected under
  different weather conditions without accounting for detectability.
- On 10% of surveys, have two observers independently record
  pollinators on the same transect to assess inter-observer agreement.
- Record floral density and dominant flowering species at every survey;
  pollinator abundance is strongly influenced by floral resource
  availability.
- For pan traps, inspect bowls mid-deployment if wind or wildlife
  disturbance is likely. Refill or replace tipped bowls and note
  the interruption.
- Voucher-pin at least 5 representative specimens per functional group
  per site per season for the reference collection.

## 10. Training Record

Before conducting pollinator surveys independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd)
   in full
2. Disclose any Hymenoptera allergy to the field lead and carry an
   EpiPen if prescribed
3. Demonstrate identification of the 10 pollinator functional groups
   (Section 6.4) using pinned specimens or photographs
4. Participate in a supervised transect observation survey and pan trap
   deployment
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
